14643-the-farmer-boy-the-story-of-jacob:
J. H. Willard's 1905 children's book, in Altemus' Children of the Bible series, retells the story of Jacob for young readers, with illustrations. The series also covered Isaac, Joseph, Moses, and David.

Jacob tricks Esau out of his birthright and blessing, and Esau cries out bitterly for a blessing of his own, while Isaac, moved by his distress, blesses him differently. Willard tells the Genesis tale in simple prose. The book is a gentle Sunday-school retelling, meant to bring a patriarch's story within a child's reach. Altemus issued the series in small illustrated volumes.
2077-the-nabob:
Alphonse Daudet, in W. Blaydes's translation, tells of a nabob, a man grown rich in the East who returns to Paris to buy power, friends, and a place in society. His fortune opens doors, but it cannot buy respect. Daudet based the nabob on rich returnees from the colonies, a familiar Paris type.

Daudet, long slow to win English readers, writes Parisian home life with warmth and sharp eyes, and his hero's rise and fall expose the market in titles and favours. The novel remains a lively satire on money and ambition. Blaydes's translation brought Daudet to English readers who had missed him in French.
20978-a-hungarian-nabob:
Too many episodes crowd A Hungarian Nabob, its translator owns with a frank plea. She begs Mor Jokai's pardon, keen the tale should charm at first sight. The English text of 1899 trims the growth for new readers' sake.

Jokai's nabob, a rich Hungarian of vast lands and wilder whims, stars here. Old Hungary's feasts, duels, pride, and reforms swirl around his house. Jokai poured his nation's life into huge, warm novels of this kind. This one, his most famed abroad, shows why Hungary crowned him its national storyteller in his own lifetime.
21005-shorty-mccabe-on-the-job:
Do things just happen, or is there a scheme on file somewhere, Shorty McCabe asks. Sewell Ford's 1913 tales put that brash query in Shorty's own slangy mouth. White hopes, trunk murders, and fire heroes crowd his comic roll of the age.

Shorty, a stocky ex-boxer turned gym keeper, meets New York life head-on here. Ford writes in a fast, funny vernacular that won vast fans in his day. Crooks, swells, and soft hearts cross Shorty's mats in quick tales. The book is pure period fun, with a shrewd, kind core beneath its wise-cracking New York surface.
2171-brother-jacob:
George Eliot tells a comic tale of Brother Jacob, a confectioner's apprentice whose love of sweets leads him astray. The son of a yeoman, fed on salt pork and dumplings, dreams of a paradise of sugared almonds and pink lozenges. Eliot wrote Brother Jacob in 1860, as a light piece between her great novels.

Eliot follows Jacob's folly with gentle irony, showing how a small appetite can shape a life. The short story charms as a minor Eliot, witty, moral, and fond of human weakness. The confectionery joke, sweet to a boy and sickening to a man, carries a moral about appetite.
25688-the-transformation-of-job:
Frederick Vining Fisher writes this tale of the high Sierras, The Transformation of Job, published by David C. Cook in Elgin and Chicago in 1900. His preface invites readers to tramp the Sierras with staff in hand, where they will find Yosemite, Gold City, and Pine Tree Ranch under other names.

Quaint characters of the tale still dwell among vine clad hills, Fisher says, and he writes to introduce friends who interested him and to tell anew the story of the human soul. Out of love for Pine Tree Ranch memories, he dedicates the book to the host who once welcomed him there.
29374-the-gaunt-gray-wolf-a-tale-of-adve:
Dillon Wallace's 1914 tale, issued in the Boy Scout Every Boy's Library, sends Shad Trowbridge of Boston north to the wilds with Ungava Bob. The lure of the wilderness draws the city boy to trails, rivers, and camps far from home. There he meets old friends, Indian attack, and a gaunt gray wolf that haunts the tale. Chapters move from rescue to river tilts, spirit voices, and a quest for vengeance.

Wallace writes for boys who dream of the North: hard travel, loyal comrades, and danger faced with pluck. The book carries the era's rough, outdoor code, with its perils and its prejudices intact. Young readers and fans of old adventure tales will find a sturdy, fast-moving story of the Canadian wilds.
29945-jan-and-her-job:
L. Allen Harker published Jan and Her Job in New York in 1917, with Charles Scribner's Sons. Jan heads the first chapter, and Jan's mail and Bombay follow. The beginning of the job, the children, and the shadow before shape the early tale. The human touch, the end of the dream, and Meg carry it forward, with plans, the state of Peter, and the wheels of chance in the middle.

Peter tells Jan in the frontispiece scene that he is her job, part of it anyway. Meg and Captain Middleton, the young idea, and two ways of love follow, with an encampment, tactics, and a demonstration in force. A chapter dated August 1914 closes the book's world on the edge of war. Harker writes a warm, capable heroine's tale of work, children, and love.
30526-illustrations-of-the-book-of-job:
William Blake's Illustrations of the Book of Job appear in a new edition published in New York in 1903, reproduced in reduced facsimile from Blake's original edition of 1826. Blake invented and engraved the plates himself, and the title page dates the London issue to 8 March 1825, from Fountain Court, Strand.

Plates pair Blake's images with lines from Job, opening with the Lord's Prayer and the note that Job feared God and eschewed evil. The volume lets readers study Blake's visual reading of suffering, patience, and divine mystery in sequence. It serves art lovers, Blake students, and Bible readers who want the engravings close to their first form.
40470-expositor-s-bible-the-book-of-job:
Book of Job in the Expositor's Bible is a commentary by Robert Watson. Funk and Wagnalls published it in New York in the year 1900. Watson also wrote Judges and Ruth and Gospels of Yesterday. A prologue treats the author and his work, then the opening scenes. Earth first, then heaven, frames the drama of Job's sore trial.

Chapters pass to the shadow of God's hand and the dilemma of faith. Three colloquies structure the long debate between Job and his friends. Eliphaz tells the things he had seen in the first colloquy round. Heads name the thought of a daysman and a witness in heaven. My Redeemer Liveth stands as a famed chapter title in the second.
42128-the-edinburgh-new-philosophical-jo:
The Edinburgh New Philosophical Journal, volume forty-nine, covering April to October, is a number of the science journal conducted by Robert Jameson. Jameson was professor of natural history at the University of Edinburgh and keeper of its museum. The title page lists his many fellowships at home and abroad, from the Royal Societies of London and Edinburgh to bodies in Berlin, Naples, and Paris.

The journal's subtitle promises a view of the newest finds and gains in the sciences and the arts. Such numbers gathered papers on geology, natural history, and kindred subjects for learned readers. Jameson's long roll of honors, filling the title page, marks the standing the journal held in its day.
51203-a-coffin-for-jacob:
Edward Ludwig's Coffin for Jacob ran in Galaxy Science Fiction in May 1956, with illustrations by Emsh. Ben Curtis enters the Blast Inn, a Venusian gin mill, with a dead man following silently behind him. The room steams with tobacco smoke and the fumes of Martian Devil's Egg. A small Martian boy, eager-eyed with pipestem limbs, offers him a pretty friend, the House of Dreams, and a good table. The price named is five dollars or twenty keelis.

Ben wants none of it: no opium, no kali, no girl. What he would buy, at the price of his soul, is a drug to bring a dead man to life. CO2-breathing Venusians, gray and scaly, stand motionless in the smoke like toads in human shape. A Security Police officer from Hoover City patrols the aisles with a neuro-club.
51595-stirring-incidents-in-the-life-of-:
Stirring Incidents in the Life of a British Soldier is the autobiography of Thomas Faughnan, a sergeant. Faughnan served late as colour sergeant in the Sixth Royal Regiment's second battalion. The third edition came out at Toronto in eighteen eighty one. He dedicates the book, by leave, to the governor general of Canada.

In his preface Faughnan says no man should write his life before middle age. Only then can the past be seen whole, as in a picture held at distance. He writes in a plain, homely style for common readers and old comrades. His schooling was a common Irish one, with no classical finish to show. He picks the chief events of his service and tells them straight. Narrow escapes, marches, and the deeds of his comrades fill the pages.
59124-the-horse-and-his-rider-or-sketche:
The Horse and His Rider is a book of sketches on the horse. Rollo Springfield wrote it, out in London in the year 1847. Its full name adds tales of the horse and of horse lands. The first part takes up how the horse was tamed by man.

That tame is the best gain man made from the beast world, it holds. Breeds, blood stock, and the small horse are set out in that part. The face of the horse and his wits fill the next part of the book. Tales show his truth to man and his love of his own kind. Bad traits, speed, and flesh as food are weighed in their turn. Wild herds of the steppes and the horse folk of the east close the run. The book loves its theme and tells it with warmth throughout.
59536-captain-lucy-and-lieutenant-bob:
Aline Havard wrote a war tale for young readers, printed in Philadelphia in 1920. Ralph Coleman drew the pictures. Havard had written Captain Lucy in France before this sequel. Lucy serves near the front, and a front picture asks if the twenty eighth will go over this week.

Marian arrives, a parade follows, and the mystery of the twenty eighth deepens. Lieutenant Bob takes his orders and says his good byes. Later chapters put the young folk over the trenches and behind the enemy lines. First aid, a gust of wind, and tough jobs test their nerve. The tale gives girls of its day a heroine in uniform at the heart of the war.
59665-a-toothache-on-zenob:
Boyd Ellanbee wrote A Toothache on Zenob for Worlds of If in October nineteen fifty-eight. A headnote muses that other eyes, twenty light-years off, see our own sun blazing in a familiar constellation. Pehn Karn sits in a signal dome on distant Zenob. His friend adjusts the dials of a receiver beside him.

Recording tape spills over the table in loops of aluminium. Doesn't this job get dull, Pehn asks, between scans. Routine space-sweep, his friend owns, but the noise from space is amazingly varied. One more sector to scan tonight, and the watch is done. Then he turns: what is the matter with you, Pehn, your face looks lop-sided. A toothache at the edge of the stars grounds Ellanbee's joke.
68189-independence-rectorial-address-del:
Rudyard Kipling gave Independence as his rectorial address at Saint Andrews. He spoke to the students there on October tenth, nineteen hundred twenty three. Doubleday, Page and Company issued the speech at Garden City in nineteen hundred twenty four. Old age preaches at youth: that jest opens his grave theme.

When young he sat and bore such preaching, Kipling owns with a smile. Now he hands on the sacred torch of boredom in his turn. A Burns verse gives his text: the grand right of being free of want. Gear is not for hoards or show, but to stand on one’s own feet. Thrift may seem stale talk in a Scots school of strict homes. Duncan of Ruthwell and Chalmers taught that school its care. Look at both sides of each coin, their households trained them. Kipling bids the young men prize self rule above each prize.
71315-how-to-get-an-air-job:
Jack Byrne wrote a guide to getting an air job. If you have the nerve and ambition to become a cloudman, this will tell you where to go to bat and how, the first page cries. In clipper ship days the youth of America heard the call of the sea, the whistle of a hurricane through the shrouds and surf on a coral shore.

Then came the call of the West, the pioneer spirit of Kit Carson and Boone. Clerks put down their pens and joined the wagon trains. The sea first, then the land, and now the last great frontier, the air. Heavier than air craft had grown from trial toys to a trade in one lifetime. Byrne tells young men what air work pays and how to break in.
75778-the-book-of-job:
The Book of Job in the Authorized Version is reprinted here in a first edition of 1916 from London, with an opening essay by Chesterton and color pictures by Mary Tongue. The text keeps the old Bible wording, with a new layout meant to aid reading. A list of eight plates shows key scenes from the story.

Job is a rich and upright man in the land of Uz, with seven sons, three daughters, and vast flocks. Loss strips him of wealth, children, and health, and friends come to debate why good men suffer. His wife urges him to curse God and die, but Job holds fast. In the end God answers from the whirlwind and restores his fortunes.
8245-the-world-english-bible-web-job:
Job was a wealthy, upright man who lost his children, his wealth, and his health in quick succession, and this ancient book asks why good people suffer. His three friends insist he must have sinned and should confess, while Job holds fast to his innocence and demands an audience with God. Their long debate fills most of the book, circling the same hard question from every side.

At last God answers, not with reasons, but with a tour of creation: wild beasts, storms, and sea monsters that dwarf human wisdom. Job yields, and his fortunes are restored. Readers still turn to Job when easy answers fail, because it honors grief and anger instead of scolding them, and leaves the mystery of suffering intact.
britannica-1911-abbadie-jakob:
Jakob Abbadie receives a life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Abbadie, a Swiss Protestant divine born at Nay in Bern, took his doctorate in theology at seventeen. Berlin heard him preach to a French church before Marshal Schomberg carried him to England in 1688.

London gave him the French church in the Savoy, and his pen defended the Revolution in print. A history of the 1696 conspiracy plot followed. King William raised him to the deanery of Killaloe in Ireland. Treatises made his wide name: on the truth of the Christian religion, on the divinity of Jesus Christ, and on self-knowledge. Texts in French ran across Europe in translation. He died in London in 1727.
britannica-1911-abbott-jacob:
Jacob Abbott receives a life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Abbott, an American writer for the young born in Maine in 1803, taught mathematics at Amherst before founding schools in Boston and New York. Preaching, school-keeping, and writing filled his working life in turns.

More than two hundred volumes bear his name. The Rollo books, twenty-eight in all, made him famous: Rollo at Work, at Play, and in Europe taught two generations of American children. Franconia stories and his makers-of-history set, written with his brother John, sold in vast numbers. The Young Christian reached adult readers. Four sons, lawyers and clergy among them, wrote as well. He died at Farmington, Maine, in 1879.
britannica-1911-albright-jacob:
Albright, Jacob, an American clergyman of 1759 to 1808, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born near Pottstown, Pennsylvania, in May 1759, he was of Pennsylvania-German parentage and his name was originally Albrecht. Educated in the Lutheran faith, he worked as a tile-burner in his early years. His life turned in 1790, when he was converted to Methodism.

In 1796 Albright resolved to preach that faith among the Pennsylvania Germans, and his efforts met with great success. By 1800 he had founded what was virtually a new, independent church on the Methodist system. He became its presiding elder and, in 1807, its bishop. The church is officially the Evangelical Association, though its people were called New Methodists, Albrights, and Albright Brethren. He died at Muhlbach, Pennsylvania, in May 1808, a year after reaching the bishop's office.
britannica-1911-arcadelt-jacob:
Jacob Arcadelt (c. 1514–c. 1556) was a Netherlands composer. He belonged to music's early Golden Age. In 1539 he left a Florence position. St Peter's in Rome needed a chorister teacher. He became one of the papal singers in 1540. Church composition made him prolific generally. His Italian publications were all madrigals, though. Five books of them appeared at Venice.

Those madrigals stimulated the Venetian school considerably. In 1555 he left Italy permanently. Cardinal Charles of Lorraine took his service. That patron was duke of Guise. Three volumes of masses followed in France. Motets went into various collections too. A famous Ave Maria bears his name. Liszt transcribed it for piano. Its attribution is doubtful, the entry warns. No source earlier than Bishop's edition traces it.
britannica-1911-ayrer-jakob:
Ayrer, Jakob (died 1605), was a German dramatist of whom little is known. He seems to have come to Nuremberg as a boy. He worked his way up to imperial notary there. He died at Nuremberg in March 1605. A rhymed chronicle of Bamberg and a Psalm translation stand beside his plays.

His Opus Theatricum, printed in 1618, holds thirty tragedies and comedies plus thirty-six Shrovetide plays and song plays. Ayrer followed Hans Sachs, but touring English actors taught him lively incident, spectacle, and the clown. Still, the entry judges his plays hardly more truly dramatic than Sachs's, and weaker in poetry. Two of his comedy plots share sources with Shakespeare's Much Ado about Nothing and The Tempest.
britannica-1911-balde-jakob:
Jakob Balde (1604–1668) was a German writer of Latin verse, born at Ensisheim in Alsace. Driven out by the raiding bands of Count Mansfeld, he fled to Ingolstadt to study law. A disappointment in love turned him toward the church, and in 1624 he joined the Society of Jesus.

Balde taught rhetoric at Innsbruck and Ingolstadt, was ordained in 1633, and became court chaplain at Munich to the elector Maximilian I. The 1911 Britannica entry reports the high praise of his own age, which ranked him with the poets of Augustan Rome. His works fill four volumes in the Cologne edition of 1650, and eight in a later Munich one.
britannica-1911-bell-jacob:
Jacob Bell (1810–1859) was a British chemist who worked to raise the standing of pharmacy. Born in London, he joined his father’s Oxford Street business and heard lectures at the Royal Institution and King’s College. At a public meeting in April 1841 his plan produced the Pharmaceutical Society of Great Britain.

Bell also founded the Pharmaceutical Journal and ran it for eighteen years, while the society gained a royal charter in 1843. He fought the practice of pharmacy by unqualified hands and drafted a reform bill in 1845. Elected for St Albans in 1850, he carried a weakened version of that bill into law before dying in 1859.
britannica-1911-bernays-jakob:
Jakob Bernays (1824–1881), a German philologist and philosophical writer born at Hamburg, studied at Bonn under Welcker and Ritschl, whose favourite pupil he became. The 1911 Britannica entry follows him to the chair of classical philology at the Jewish theological college at Breslau in 1853, and back to Bonn in 1866 as professor and chief librarian.

His works deal mainly with the Greek philosophers: studies of Aristotle's dialogues and dramatic theory, Theophrastus on piety, the Heraclitean letters, and Lucian and the Cynics. He remained at Bonn until his death in 1881. The article also sketches his brother Michael, a literary historian who, unlike Jakob, embraced Christianity.
britannica-1911-berzelius-jons-jakob:
Jöns Jakob Berzelius (1779–1848) was a Swedish chemist, born near Linköping. He studied chemistry and medicine at Upsala and took his medical degree in 1802. That year he became assistant professor of botany and pharmacy at Stockholm. Full professor rank followed in 1807. From 1815 to 1832 he taught chemistry at the Caroline institution. The Stockholm Academy made him its perpetual secretary in 1818.

His life's work was fixing the composition of chemical compounds. The 1911 Britannica entry ties this to the law of multiple proportions and atomic theory. He spent ten years pinning down atomic and molecular weights. He isolated elements such as selenium, silicon, and thorium for the first time. He published over 250 memoirs, a five-edition textbook, and 27 annual report volumes.
britannica-1911-bodmer-johann-jakob:
Johann Jakob Bodmer is the subject of a life story in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Bodmer was a Swiss German author who lived from 1698 to 1783. He was born near Zurich. After studying church subjects and trying trade, he found his calling in letters. In 1725 he became professor of Swiss history at Zurich. He held that chair for half a century.

The article notes his weekly journal, modelled on the Spectator, printed in the early seventeen twenties. His prose translation of Milton's Paradise Lost in 1732 opened English writing to German readers. That work drew hostile attack from Gottsched and his school, a fight Bodmer won in full. His key treatises plead for freedom of the imagination against French rules. His own epics and plays are judged weak. His editions of old German singers and epic verse did lasting service. He died at Zurich in 1783.
britannica-1911-brucker-johann-jakob:
Johann Jakob Brucker (1696–1770) was a German historian of philosophy born at Augsburg and destined for the church. He graduated at the University of Jena in 1718, returned to Augsburg in 1720, became parish minister of Kaufbeuren in 1723. In 1731 was elected to the Berlin Academy of Sciences and called back to Augsburg as pastor and senior minister of St Ulrich's church.

His chief work, Historia Critica Philosophiae, appeared at Leipzig in five volumes from 1742 to 1744, succeeded so well that a six-volume edition followed in 1766-1767 and an English translation by W. Enfield in 1791. It is by this work alone that he is now known. Its merit lies wholly in its ample collection of materials. Other writings include a history of the doctrine of ideas and Kurze Fragen, a seven-volume history of philosophy in question and answer form holding literary details his chief work omitted.
britannica-1911-bryant-jacob:
Jacob Bryant (1715–1804) was an English antiquarian. He wrote on ancient mythology. This 1911 Britannica entry traces his life and books. He was born at Plymouth. He went to school near Rochester and then to Eton. In 1736 he won a scholarship to King's College, Cambridge. Later he tutored the duke of Marlborough. He then served the duke as private secretary in Germany. A well-paid ordnance post left him leisure for study.

The entry lists his main works in turn. First came Observations and Inquiries on ancient history, in 1767. Then came A New System, an analysis of ancient mythology. That book, from 1774 to 1776, is called fantastic and now valueless. Bryant also defended Josephus and the scriptures in print. He argued that the Trojan War never took place. He died near Windsor on 14 November 1804. He left his library to King's College.
britannica-1911-camerarius-rudolf-jakob: Rudolf Jakob Camerarius was a German plant man and healer who lived from sixteen sixty-five to seventeen twenty-one. He was born at Tubingen. In sixteen eighty-seven he became a teacher of the heal art there and head of its plant grounds. His fame rests on his work on how plants breed. A note from him on that theme came out in sixteen ninety-four. The entry here is brief and gives little more than dates, posts, and that one famed note.
britannica-1911-carstens-armus-jacob:
Armus Jacob Carstens (1754–1798) is the subject of a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on a German painter born in Schleswig. He went to Copenhagen to study in 1776. In 1783 he travelled to Italy, where the work of Giulio Romano impressed him deeply. He then settled in Lübeck and worked as a portrait painter.

Help from friends let Carstens visit Rome again in 1792, and there he gradually produced fine subject and historical paintings. Works such as “Plato's Symposium” and the “Battle of Rossbach” made his name. He was appointed professor at Berlin, and in 1795 a large exhibition of his works was held in Rome. He died in that city in 1798. The entry ranks him as the founder of the later school of German historical painting, a standing his Roman exhibition had already announced in his lifetime.
britannica-1911-cats-jacob:
Jacob Cats was a Dutch poet and humorist of the seventeenth century. He lived from fifteen seventy seven to sixteen sixty. His life entry appears in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born at Brouwershaven in Zeeland, he lost his mother at an early age.

Cats studied law at Leiden and at Orleans, then practised at the Hague. His defence of a poor woman charged with witchcraft won him clients. A long fever broke a planned marriage and defied cure for two years. A wandering quack cured him in Zeeland in a strange turn. He wed Elisabeth von Valkenburg in sixteen o two and turned to farming. His best works join emblem poems with plain moral verse for homes.
britannica-1911-crusenstolpe-magnus-jako:
Magnus Jakob Crusenstolpe, who lived from 1795 to 1865, was a Swedish historian. An entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica weighs his sharp pen and bias. He won early fame as a writer on politics and the past. His first big work told the early life of a Swedish king.

For three years the king gave Crusenstolpe his full trust. The writer paper backed the crown as an official voice. In 1833 he turned and attacked the king without rest. One fierce piece earned him three years in a castle prison in 1838. He kept writing until his death in 1865. Few Swedes wrote with so clean and cutting a style. But party hate bends his history, the entry warns.
britannica-1911-elvey-sir-george-job:
Elvey, Sir George Job (1816–1893), was an English organist and composer born at Canterbury on 27 March 1816. He sang as a chorister at Canterbury cathedral under Highmore Skeats. He then studied under his elder brother Stephen and at the Royal Academy of Music. In 1834 he gained the Gresham prize medal for his anthem “Bow down thine ear.”

In 1835 Elvey became organist of St George's chapel, Windsor, a post he filled for 47 years, retiring in 1882. He took the Oxford degrees of Mus.B. in 1838 and Mus.D. in 1840. Anthems of his were ordered for the Three Choirs Festivals of 1853 and 1857. He received a knighthood in 1871 and died at Windlesham in Surrey on 9 December 1893. His works are nearly all for the Church, with two oratorios, many anthems and services, and some organ pieces.
britannica-1911-frauenlob:
Frauenlob was the name by which Heinrich von Meissen, a German poet of the 13th century, is generally known. Born about 1250 to a humble burgher family, he is said to have won the name in a song contest with his rival Regenbogen. There he defended the word Frau, lady, against Weib, woman. His youth was poor, but courts across Germany came to want his singing.

He rode with Rudolph I in the Marchfeld in 1278 and stood at Prague in 1286 for the knighting of Wenceslaus II. In 1311 he was at a festival held by Waldemar of Brandenburg, then settled at Mainz, where popular account credits him with founding the first school of Meistersingers. He died in 1318 and lies in the cloisters of Mainz cathedral. His poems show wide learning and delight in far-fetched images and tricks of rhyme.
britannica-1911-frohschammer-jakob:
Jakob Frohschammer (1821-1893), German theologian and philosopher, was born at Illkofen near Regensburg on 6 January 1821. Meant for the priesthood, he studied theology at Munich yet felt drawn to philosophy. In 1847 he took what he called the most mistaken step of his life and was ordained. His logical mind sat badly with the obedience the Church demanded.

His 1850 church history was placed on the Index, and in 1855 he became professor of philosophy. His book on the origin of human souls argued the soul comes by a secondary creative act of the parents. Later works attacked the Thomist claim that philosophy serves theology and defended the freedom of science. The pope denounced him in 1862 and students were barred from his lectures, yet king and students backed him. Excommunicated in 1871, he built his later system on imagination as the ground of the world process.
britannica-1911-geel-jacob:
Jacob Geel (1789–1862) was a Dutch scholar and critic born at Amsterdam on the 12th of November 1789. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica records his posts at Leiden: under librarian in 1823, then chief librarian and honorary professor in 1833. He held those posts until his death there on the 11th of November 1862.

Geel did much to build up classical studies in Holland. He edited Theocritus in 1820, the Vatican fragments of Polybius in 1829, and the Olympic speech of Dio Chrysostom in 1840. He helped found a leading review of criticism and wrote many essays for learned journals. He also made a prized catalogue of the manuscripts in the Leiden library and wrote a history of the Greek sophists. German works turned into Dutch by his hand spread his influence further.
britannica-1911-haynau-julius-jacob:
Julius Jacob Haynau (1786–1853) was an Austrian general. He was the natural son of William IX of Hesse-Cassel. He entered the Austrian army as an infantry officer in 1801. Wagram wounded him during the Napoleonic wars. Italy in 1813 and 1814 distinguished him. By 1847 he was a field marshal lieutenant. A violent, uncontrolled temper troubled his superiors. His hatred of revolution was fanatical.

In 1848 that zeal marked him for command in Italy. His suppression of the Brescia rising was notoriously severe. The mob had first massacred invalid Austrian soldiers there. Hungary called him in June 1849. Rapid successes against the Hungarians followed. Accusations of brutality followed him there too. Quarrels with the war minister ended his command in 1850. London draymen attacked him at a brewery visit. He died on 14 March 1853.
britannica-1911-henle-friedrich-gustav-j:
Friedrich Gustav Jakob Henle (1809–1885) was a German pathologist and anatomist. He was born at Fürth in Franconia on 9 July 1809. Heidelberg and Bonn gave him his medical studies. His doctor's degree came in 1832. He became prosector to Johannes Müller at Berlin. Six years there produced anatomical monographs and papers. Epithelium, lacteals, hair, mucus and pus engaged him. Zürich gave him the anatomy chair in 1840.

Heidelberg called him in 1844 to teach anatomy, physiology and pathology. His Manual of Rational Pathology began in 1846. It treated physiology and pathology as branches of one science. Göttingen received him in 1852. His Handbook of Systematic Human Anatomy issued from 1855. Its last volume appeared only in 1873. His researches were mainly histological in character. He died at Göttingen on 13 May 1885. Note: this record's hosted file is a shared page chunk; the Henle entry stands complete within it.
britannica-1911-herzog-johann-jakob:
Johann Jakob Herzog (1805–1882) was a German Protestant theologian, born at Basel on the 12th of September 1805. He studied at Basel and Berlin, and in 1854 settled at Erlangen as professor of church history. He retired in 1877 and died at Erlangen on the 30th of September 1882. His name rests chiefly on one vast work of reference.

That work is the Realencyklopädie für protestantische Theologie und Kirche, published in 22 volumes between 1853 and 1868. In 1877 Herzog began a new edition with G. L. Plitt, and after Plitt's death Albert Hauck carried it on. Hauck started the third edition in 1896, and it was completed in 22 volumes in 1909. Herzog's other books include lives and studies such as Joh. Calvin (1843), Leben Ökolampads (1843) and Die romanischen Waldenser (1853). His Abriss der gesamten Kirchengeschichte filled three volumes (1876–1882).
britannica-1911-heyne-christian-gottlob:
Christian Gottlob Heyne (1729–1812) was a German classical scholar and archaeologist, born at Chemnitz in Saxony on the 25th of September 1729. His father was a poor weaver, and a godfather paid for his early schooling. He entered Leipzig university in 1748, often short of the bare needs of life. A tutorship in a French merchant's family let him finish his course, but lean years followed.

A Latin elegy caught the eye of Count von Brühl, who sent for him in April 1752. Promised a secretaryship and salary, he got instead an under-clerk's post in the count's library, at under twenty pounds a year. Translation work added to it; his Tibullus appeared in 1755 and his Epictetus in 1756. The Seven Years' War left him destitute again. The bombardment of Dresden in July 1760 destroyed his nearly finished edition of Lucian. He married in 1761, still with no fixed income.
britannica-1911-holyoake-george-jacob:
George Jacob Holyoake (1817–1906) was an English secularist and co-operator, born at Birmingham on the 13th of April 1817. He became an Owenite lecturer while young. In 1841 he was the last person convicted for blasphemy in a public lecture, though the words were only a reply to a question from the floor. He served six months in prison all the same.

On his release Holyoake coined the mild term secularism for his opinions and founded the Reasoner to back them. He was also the last person indicted for publishing an unstamped newspaper. His later years went chiefly to the co-operative movement among working people. He wrote the history of the Rochdale Pioneers (1857) and The History of Co-operation in England (1875). His autobiography, Sixty Years of an Agitator's Life, appeared in 1892. He died at Brighton in January 1906.
britannica-1911-jordaens-jacob:
Jacob Jordaens (1593-1678), a Flemish painter, is the subject of an article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was born at Antwerp and died there. Like Rubens, he studied under Adam van Noort, and in 1616 he married his master's daughter. That step kept him from a trip to Rome, the making of many painters of his age.

He contented himself with studying such Italian works as he found at home. A far stronger force on his style was Rubens, who at times set him to blow up small sketches to a large scale. The article ranks him second to Rubens alone in their branch of the Flemish school. Both share warmth of colour, truth to nature, and force of expression. Jordaens falls short, the entry says, in dignity of thought, in choice of forms, and in correct drawing. His coarse humour is saved only by its life.
britannica-1911-ludolf-hiob:
Hiob Ludolf is the subject of a life story in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Ludolf was a German scholar of the East who lived from 1624 to 1704. He was born at Erfurt and studied language at Erfurt and at Leiden. He travelled to widen his knowledge of tongues. In Italy he met an Abyssinian scholar named Gregorius. From him he gained a deep knowledge of the Ethiopian language.

The article tells how he served the duke of Saxe-Gotha from 1652 to 1678. He then retired to Frankfurt to write. In 1683 he visited England to promote a plan for trade with Abyssinia, but church hostility blocked it. He is said to have known twenty five languages. His works include a history of Ethiopia, translated into several tongues. He also wrote grammars and word books for Ethiopian tongues.
britannica-1911-moser-johann-jakob:
Johann Jakob Moser, a German law scholar born in seventeen hundred and one, is profiled in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born at Stuttgart, he studied at Tubingen. At age nineteen he was made a teacher of law there. In time he rose to a full chair at a second school.

Clashes with the Prussian king led him to quit those posts in seventeen thirty nine. He went home and gave years to study. There he wrote his great work on the state law of Germany. In seventeen fifty one he was called back to serve his own prince. Steps he took against harsh acts by that duke led to a jail term on a hill fort. He was held for five years. The life shows a law man who paid a high price for fair rule.
britannica-1911-ob:
The Ob is the subject of a river entry in the 1911 Britannica. The Ob is a great river of west Siberia. Local peoples know it by more than one name. It forms where the Biya and the Katun meet. Both streams rise in the Altai hills. One flows out of a lake and one bursts from ice. The river winds west and north on its long course.

It ends in the Gulf of Ob on the Arctic Ocean. That gulf cuts deep into the coast for miles. The Irtysh is its greatest side stream by far. More streams join it from the right and the left. Boats can use a vast web of waters in its basin. A canal web links the Ob with the Yenisei. Ice locks the river for months each year. Steam boats have worked its mid course since 1845.
britannica-1911-paulus-heinrich-eberhard:
Heinrich Eberhard Gottlob Paulus, a German church scholar who lived from 1761 to 1851, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born at Leonberg near Stuttgart, he studied at Tubingen and taught in a German school. He then spent two years on tour in England, Holland, and France. In 1789 he became a chair holder in eastern tongues at Jena.

Paulus is known for a plain, natural way of reading the Bible. He held that tales of wonders join a true fact to the view the writer took of it. His Life of Jesus came out in 1828, and his large notes on the New Testament ran to four books. Later chairs took him to Wurzburg and then to Heidelberg, where he taught until 1844.
britannica-1911-perkins-jacob:
Jacob Perkins, an American inventor who lived from 1766 to 1849, is profiled in a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica article. Born at Newburyport in Massachusetts, he was apprenticed to a goldsmith. He soon made his name with a range of useful mechanical inventions. In 1818 he came to England with a plan for engraving bank notes on steel.

The entry says that plan proved a clear success, carried out with the English engraver Heath. His chief gift to physics lay in trials that proved water can be compressed. He measured that effect with a pressure gauge of his own invention. The article closes with his son and grandson, who also worked on steam. One devised a way to warm buildings with high pressure steam.
britannica-1911-spener-philipp-jakob:
Philipp Jakob Spener, a German theologian who lived from 1635 to 1705, is profiled in a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica article. Born at Rappoltsweiler in Upper Alsace, he went to Strassburg in 1651 to study language, history, and philosophy. He won his master's degree in 1653 with a defence against the thought of Hobbes. He then tutored two princes and lectured at the university.

From 1659 to 1662 he visited other universities, among them Basel, Tubingen, and Geneva. At Geneva his religious views turned toward mysticism, the entry stresses. Back at Strassburg he became a preacher with leave to lecture. Three years later he was called as chief pastor of the Lutheran church at Frankfurt. There he issued his two chief works in later years.
britannica-1911-steiner-jakob:
Jakob Steiner (1796-1863) was a Swiss mathematician, and his life and work are set out in an entry from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born at Utzendorf in the canton of Bern, he became a pupil of Pestalozzi at eighteen, then studied at Heidelberg. He went to Berlin, living by private lessons.

The entry tells how a new chair of geometry was founded for him at Berlin in 1834, which he held until his death. His work was confined to geometry, which he treated by synthesis alone, hating analysis. In his own field he surpassed all his contemporaries, and he is rated the greatest geometrical genius since Apollonius.
britannica-1911-sturm-von-sturmeck-jacob:
Jacob Sturm von Sturmeck, who lived from 1489 to 1553, was a German statesman and reformer. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica opens with his birth at Strassburg. He studied at Heidelberg and Freiburg universities. About 1517 he entered the service of the provost of Strassburg. The reformed doctrines soon won him over. In 1524 he joined the governing body of his home city. He steered its policy through the Peasants' War.

At diet after diet he pled his city's cause with fame. He signed the famous protest at Spires in 1529. That act made him one of the first men called Protestants. He pushed for union among the reform parties. When union talks failed, he laid a Zwinglian confession before the Augsburg diet. His sway brought Strassburg into the Schmalkaldic league in 1531. After its defeat he won mild terms from the emperor.
brother-jacob:
George Eliot told a small, sharp tale in Brother Jacob, a short novel of a confectioner with a secret. David Faux, a yeoman's son, chose the sweet trade for its sugared almonds and lozenges, then soured on its low standing. Ambitious and full of contrivance, David steals, reinvents himself under a new name, and rises in a new town.

His rise depends on nobody knowing his past, and his simple-minded brother Jacob, fond of animals and sweet things, is the past in person. When Jacob wanders into his brother's new life, the comedy turns cruel and then just. Eliot packs her themes of ambition, class shame, and consequence into a tale readable at one sitting.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jacob:
Jacob, son of Isaac and Rebekah, was the third great patriarch of the chosen people. He became the immediate ancestor of Israel's twelve tribes. His life appears in Genesis 25 to 50. Modern scholars split that text into documents labeled J, E, and P. His name, possibly short for Jacob-El, means supplanter. It points to a well-known event at his birth.

His early years were marked by efforts to win Esau's birthright. That struggle began before birth, the text says. Later he bought the birthright for lentil pottage when Esau was faint. Then, by a ruse, he won Isaac's blessing meant for Esau. To escape his brother's anger he fled. The entry follows a patriarch whose cunning and blessing shaped a nation's origin story.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-job:
Job is both a book of the Old Testament and its chief figure, and this entry treats the book first, with the man as occasion allows. Eleven heads organise it: place in the canon, authority, characters, contents, arrangement of the poem, design, teaching on life after death, integrity, text, the author's skill and metre, and date.

In Hebrew Bibles Psalms, Proverbs, and Job stand together in the Writings, Job between or after the other two, while Greek and Latin Bibles place it before Psalms.  after the histories. Old lists vary widely, and the Syriac Bible sets it right after the Pentateuch. That shifting place mirrors the book's own puzzle: why the just suffer, and what answer, if any, the poem gives.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-mesrob:
Mesrob, also called Mashtots, stands among the greatest figures in Armenian history. He was born about 361 at Hassik in Taron province and died at Valarsabad in 441. Son of Vartan of the Mamikonian family, he won a liberal education, versed in Greek, Syriac, and Persian, by his pupil Goriun's account. For his piety and learning he became secretary to King Chosroes III, writing royal decrees in Greek, Persian, and Syriac letters, since Armenia then had no national alphabet.

 Leaving court for God's service, he took Holy Orders and withdrew to a monastery with chosen companions. There, says Goriun, he bore great austerities. Hunger and thirst, cold and poverty, living on vegetables, wearing a hair shirt, sleeping on the ground, and often spending whole nights in prayer and Scripture study. He kept this life for some years, readying himself for the great work Providence soon set him, giving Armenia its alphabet.
doe-osti-2571779-cryogenic-optical-and-s:
A final technical report dated July 2025, from Advanced Research Systems under SBIR award DE-SC0021513 with Ravi Bains as principal investigator, describes a cryogenic probe station for studying quantum defects in solids. The instrument, nicknamed Avalanche, scans samples at temperatures from 4 to 300 kelvin inside an ultra-high vacuum chamber. It pairs an atomic force microscope with light-based tools for near-field and far-field spectroscopy.

Building the cryostat proved to be the hard part. Paper-thin steel tubes, scarce specialist welders, and imported high-grade copper each caused long delays when anything failed. The design went through three rounds with collaborators at the University of Colorado Boulder. The Department of Energy cancelled the award in 2024, yet the company finished the system on its own research budget. Final cryogenic checks came first, with the microscope's system test set for August 2025.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-CohenJacob_Cohe:
Jacob Cohen, a historian, wrote for The Nation an article titled 'The Vital Documents,' on the Kennedy assassination's documentary record. This letter, dated July 3, 1966, was written to Cohen about that article.

The Nation's pages were a battleground of the first assassination debate, where critics and defenders of the Warren Commission traded charges about which documents mattered and what they proved. A letter like this one is the debate at ground level: one reader, one article, and the argument joined by mail. The letter is preserved as part of the correspondence the controversy generated.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-GibbonsBob_Gibb: A letter from Bob Gibbons to a man named Gary, whose surname is illegible, concerns the Zapruder film, the home movie of the Kennedy assassination. The date attached to the letter in the record reads May 12, 1960, which cannot be right for a film shot in 1963 and is best treated as a garbled date. The letter survives as a researcher's note about the famous film.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-VernonBob_Verno: Michael Hytha wrote about Bob Vernon, a lone television maker from Antioch, and an Illinois inmate who claimed Vernon's support. Vernon had come to believe in evidence that challenged the official account of the Kennedy assassination. The article follows a small, stubborn corner of assassination research, far from Washington and the big publishers. It shows how belief in the case spread through local media figures.
tanakh-jps-1917-job:
Job is a wisdom book of the Hebrew Bible, presented in the 1917 Jewish Publication Society translation of the Holy Scriptures. It opens in the land of Uz with a man named Job, praised as whole-hearted, upright, and one who shunned evil.

Job holds vast wealth, with seven sons, three daughters, and herds that make him the greatest man of the east. He offers gifts for his children after each feast, lest they have sinned in their hearts. Then the sons of God come before the Lord, and Satan comes among them. Readers enter the Bible's deep test of why the just suffer, told in prose frames and long, fierce verse debate.
the-farmer-boy-the-story-of-jacob:
J. H. Willard retold the Bible story of Jacob for young readers in The Farmer Boy, part of Altemus' Children of the Bible series, printed at Philadelphia in 1905. Jacob stands in a line of boy heroes from Isaac to the boy Jesus.

The tale opens with Abraham, head of the Hebrew tribe, moving with flocks, herds, camels, and servants from place to place. From that stock comes Jacob, the farmer boy of the title. Willard keeps the speech plain and the scenes short, so a child can follow the births, blessings, and tricks that shape the father of a nation.
the-nabob:
Alphonse Daudet's novel The Nabob, translated by W. Blaydes, opens with a long critical introduction rather than the story. Daudet once remarked, the introducer writes, that England was the last foreign country to welcome his novels, which surprised him, since home life mattered greatly to him and to the typical Englishman. In time he won English and American hearts more completely than any contemporary French novelist.

Admirers is too cold a word, the essay argues; friends is heartier and fits better. Some readers found in Daudet a French Dickens, others a refined Mark Twain with a flavour of Cervantes. Most simply enjoyed him, the introducer says, because his writing was steeped in his own charming personality, as a Corot picture is steeped in sunlight.
the-world-english-bible-web-job:
Job appears as book eighteen in the World English Bible, set in the land of Uz. Its hero is blameless, upright, and God-fearing. He turns away from evil, readers are told at once. Seven sons and three daughters fill his house. His wealth includes thousands of sheep and camels. He is called the greatest man in the east.

His sons feast in rotation on their birthdays. Their sisters join the celebrations. After each round Job offers burnt sacrifices for them. He worries they may have cursed God in their hearts. That careful piety makes his coming losses harder. The book then asks why the righteous suffer at all.
